newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sets meeting to review income-tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sets meeting to review income-tax reform.

text.p: Finance officials pledged on Tuesday to meet soon to review proposals to streamline Taiwan's much-maligned tax system, but would not comment on a report that the reformed income tax for business would be 35 percent.
In late June, the Finance Ministry appointed a commission to study tax reform in its drive to liberalise financial markets.
"The commission is scheduled to hold a meeting in the next few days to review various tax proposals, but the results won't be the final decision," a ministry spokesman said by telephone.
Finance Minister Paul Chiu had said the panel began work on July 1 and would complete within four months a feasibility study on a ministry plan to unify Taiwan's two income taxes.
Business leaders have complained that Taiwan's dual income tax system, in which earnings are subject to a business income tax and a personal income tax, was cumbersome and unfair.
The commission of scholars, industry leaders and officials is also looking at tariffs, business taxes on financial and insurance operations, and commodities taxes.

The local Economic Daily News said on Tuesday the ministry had completed proposals on combining the two income taxes and that the unified tax would be 35 percent for businesses compared with the current 25 percent business income tax.
Enforcing a unified tax at 25 percent would reduce state tax revenues by an annual T$21.3 billion (US$775 million), it said.

Setting the unified tax at 30 percent would trim the annual reduction to T$43 million (US$1.6 million), while a 35 percent rate would result in a net annual tax gain of T$11 billion (US$400 million), the newspaper said.
The ministry spokesman refused to comment on the report.
